solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Double served with beer for Glastonbury star (3,4)

annotation.surface: A festival-goer orders a double with a pint while watching the headliner.
annotation.walkthrough: Glastonbury is England's biggest music festival, which this pop singer headlined. The enumeration (3,4) hides where the double ends and the beer begins.
annotation.definitionFit: Dua Lipa is a pop singer who has topped the bill at Glastonbury.

entries.clue: Leaving university begin something outstanding (4)

indicatorNotes.Leaving: the U departs from the word

annotation.surface: A graduate leaves university to start a brilliant career.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' looks like praise, but here it means unpaid — a debt is money still outstanding. Remove U from DEBUT.
annotation.definitionFit: A debt is an amount still outstanding, i.e. owed.

entries.clue: Circus performer in dress almost grabbed by a lion? (7)

indicatorNotes.almost: the last letter of ROBE is dropped
indicatorNotes.grabbed by: To be grabbed by someone is to be held in their clutches, so ROB sits inside A CAT.

blocks.note: a lion is, for example, a cat; ROB goes after the C

annotation.surface: A circus act where a performer in costume is seized by the big cat.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a lion is only an example of a cat: A C(ROB)AT.
annotation.definitionFit: Acrobats, tumbling and flying on the trapeze, are a staple of the big top: a plain synonym by category.

entries.clue: One story’s no good about designated victim (5)

indicatorNotes.no good: G (good) is taken out of SAGA

blocks.note: a saga is a long story; SAGA's = SAGA has
G = good, removed from SAGA to leave SAA

annotation.surface: A crime novel with a nasty plot about a marked victim.
annotation.walkthrough: In Genesis, Abraham was told to sacrifice his son Isaac, who was spared at the last moment — so Isaac was designated as the victim.
annotation.definitionFit: Isaac was the son God told Abraham to offer as a sacrifice.

entries.clue: Basil for example a sentimental sort missing the point (8)

indicatorNotes.missing: Something missing is absent, so the N drops out of A ROMANTIC.

blocks.note: N = north, a point of the compass; removed

annotation.surface: Basil — a man's name — is described as a soppy type lacking sharpness.
annotation.walkthrough: Basil reads as a man's name, which suits 'a sentimental sort'; it is the herb. 'The point' is a compass point, here N.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: basil is one of the aromatics, the fragrant herbs cooks use, taking AROMATIC as a noun.
annotation.definitionNote: AROMATIC is used as a noun here: a fragrant plant.

entries.clue: Came around, receiving ball on right side, finding Shearer? (7)

indicatorNotes.around: To come around is to turn back on yourself, so HAILED is written in reverse.
indicatorNotes.receiving: the reversed word takes in L
indicatorNotes.right side: the right-hand end of 'ball', its last letter

blocks.note: the letter at the right-hand end of BALL

annotation.surface: A footballer comes round and gets the ball on the right wing, looking for Alan Shearer.
annotation.walkthrough: Shearer suggests Alan Shearer the England striker, fitting the football surface; here it is someone who shears. DELI(L)AH.
annotation.definitionFit: Delilah cut off Samson's hair, taking his strength — a shearer in the Bible.

entries.clue: Stone set in ring farthest from centre (6)

indicatorNotes.set in: ST is placed inside DIAL, like a gem in a setting

blocks.note: to ring = to dial a phone; ST goes after DI
st = stone, the unit of weight

annotation.surface: A jeweller sets a stone in a ring.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set in ring' makes you think of jewellery; the stone is the weight abbreviation and the ring is a phone call.
annotation.definitionFit: Distal is the anatomical term for the part farthest from the body's centre.

entries.clue: Drop proceedings in which I would never appear? (5,4)

annotation.definition: in which I would never appear?
annotation.surface: A witness hopes to drop a lawsuit they want no part of.
annotation.walkthrough: The pronoun I is always written as a capital, so it never appears in lower case.
annotation.definitionFit: Lower case is the small letters, and the pronoun I is always a capital.
annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a description of LOWER CASE rather than a synonym.

entries.clue: One always behind Labour lass on the rise (7)

indicatorNotes.on the rise: in a down clue, rising means read upwards

blocks.note: a drag = a labour, a tiresome task

annotation.surface: A political picture: someone always trailing the Labour party's rising young woman.
annotation.walkthrough: Labour with a capital looks like the political party; it is plain toil. DRAG GAL is read upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A laggard is someone who always falls behind.

entries.clue: Conservative sporting dodgy hairstyle wildly funny (10)

indicatorNotes.sporting: C wears, i.e. joins, the fodder
indicatorNotes.dodgy: HAIRSTYLE is unreliable, so its letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A Tory MP with a ridiculous haircut is a laughing stock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wildly' looks like a second anagram signal, but it belongs to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Hysterical is used informally to mean extremely funny.

entries.clue: Wild fire appearing shortly after wounding remark (9)

indicatorNotes.after: 'After' means following in order, so the fired-up piece is written behind BARB.

blocks.note: to fire (up) = to arouse; cut to AROUS

annotation.surface: A spiteful comment soon sparks a furious outburst.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue names the pieces back to front: 'appearing after' puts the fire behind the remark, so read the wordplay's second half first.
annotation.definitionFit: Barbarous means savage, uncivilised — wild.

entries.clue: Seam rolled back to cover silver screw (5)

indicatorNotes.rolled back: A thing rolled back turns over on itself, so SEW is written in reverse.
indicatorNotes.to cover: To cover is to wrap round, so the reversed seam goes around the silver.

blocks.note: to seam = to sew; reversed to WES, AG goes after W
Ag, the chemical symbol for silver

annotation.surface: A tailor turns back a seam over a silver screw.
annotation.walkthrough: Screw is British slang for wages, pay. The surface makes it a piece of hardware.
annotation.definitionFit: In British slang, a screw is someone's wage or salary.
annotation.definitionNote: Screw is singular slang; WAGES is plural in form but names the same single pay packet.

entries.clue: Sneak exiting card game left with golden award (13)

indicatorNotes.exiting: Something exiting leaves the room, so the sneak's letters walk out of the card game.

blocks.note: a rat = a sneak, an informer
the casino game; minus RAT leaves BACCA

annotation.surface: A cheat slips out of the card room clutching a gold prize.
annotation.walkthrough: AUREATE is a rare literary word for golden. The baccalaureate is the French school-leaving qualification.
annotation.definitionFit: A baccalaureate is an academic qualification awarded on completing studies.

entries.clue: Winning with Neath or Garryowen? (2-3-5)

annotation.surface: A rugby match: the Welsh club Neath or the Irish club Garryowen scoring a win.
annotation.walkthrough: Neath and Garryowen look like two rugby clubs; Neath is really 'neath, under. A Garryowen, named after the Limerick club, is a high rugby kick chased by the kicker's team.
annotation.definitionFit: An up-and-under is another name for the Garryowen, a high kick in rugby.

entries.clue: Poor film about a crime where folio goes astray (8)

indicatorNotes.about: 'About' in its sense of around: the film wraps round the crime.
indicatorNotes.goes astray: the F wanders off from A THEFT

blocks.note: a pic = a picture, a film; ATHET goes after the P
f = folio; removed to leave ATHET

annotation.surface: A critic pans a heist movie with a missing manuscript at its heart.
annotation.walkthrough: The film is PIC, the crime is A THEFT, and folio is the abbreviation F: P(A THE[F]T)IC.
annotation.definitionFit: Pathetic means miserably inadequate — poor.

entries.clue: Other son securing flat for timely break (9)

blocks.note: else = other; EVEN goes after EL

annotation.surface: Another son holds onto a flat to take a well-timed break.
annotation.walkthrough: Elevenses is a British mid-morning snack and tea break, taken at around eleven o'clock — hence 'timely'.
annotation.definitionFit: Elevenses is a break named after the hour it is taken.

entries.clue: Limits to growth set by India’s Indira? (6)

indicatorNotes.Limits to: the first and last letters of 'growth'
indicatorNotes.set by: I is placed beside the rest

blocks.note: the limits of GROWTH are G and H, spelt out as G AND H
India is I in the phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: India's prime minister Indira sets limits on the country's growth.
annotation.walkthrough: The trick is to spell out the limits literally: G AND H. 'India's' then supplies I, the phonetic-alphabet letter, and Indira is the example.
annotation.definitionFit: Indira Gandhi was prime minister of India; the question mark shows she is one example of a Gandhi.

entries.clue: This writer against himself for the moment? (8)

blocks.note: himself, i.e. the same writer, again ME

annotation.surface: A writer in two minds, arguing with himself for now.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Himself' refers back to 'this writer', so it gives ME a second time.
annotation.definitionFit: For the moment means in the meantime, the interval before something else happens.
annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a phrase meaning 'in the meantime'; MEANTIME is the noun it contains.

entries.clue: Saboteur losing heart becomes more virtuous (6)

indicatorNotes.losing heart: one of the two central Bs is dropped

blocks.note: a nobbler tampers with racehorses; minus a middle B

annotation.surface: A saboteur loses his nerve and turns good.
annotation.walkthrough: To nobble is British slang for sabotaging a racehorse or bribing a juror, so a nobbler is a saboteur.
annotation.definitionFit: Nobler means of finer moral character — more virtuous.

entries.clue: Danger lurks in Lizzy being cut near ribs (7)

indicatorNotes.lurks in: To lurk in a place is to hide inside it, so the danger hides within Lizzy's pet name.

blocks.note: Bet, a pet form of Elizabeth like Lizzy; RISK goes after B

annotation.surface: A menacing warning that Lizzy is in danger of a knife near her ribs.
annotation.walkthrough: Lizzy and Bet are both short for Elizabeth, so one pet name stands for the other.
annotation.definitionFit: Brisket is a cut of beef from the breast, next to the ribs.

entries.clue: Cook made to keep back especially grand rum (8)

indicatorNotes.Cook: MADE is cooked, i.e. its letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.to keep: To keep something is to hold it, so the cooked letters hold the grand word inside them.
indicatorNotes.back: 'Back' means backwards, so the especially grand word is written in reverse.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 4 letters; ERAR goes after DEM

annotation.surface: A chef keeps back an especially grand rum for the kitchen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cook' looks like the chef but is the anagram signal; DEM(ERAR)A. Demerara is a dark rum from Guyana, and also a brown sugar.
annotation.definitionFit: Demerara rum is distilled in Guyana, named after the Demerara river.

entries.clue: Dancing-girl with special talent announced for calendar (7)

indicatorNotes.announced: KNACK is to be heard rather than spelt

blocks.note: an alma (or almah) is an Egyptian dancing-girl
a knack is a special talent; said out, it gives NAC

annotation.surface: A showgirl with a special talent has her act listed in a calendar.
annotation.walkthrough: ALMA is a crossword stalwart: an Egyptian dancing-girl.
annotation.definitionFit: An almanac is an annual calendar with dates and information.

entries.clue: Shrew at Padua carried by ship moves across ice (6)

indicatorNotes.carried by: KATE sits inside SS, as cargo in a ship

blocks.note: SS = steamship; KATE goes after the first S
Kate is the shrew in Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, set in Padua

annotation.surface: A Shakespearean heroine carried by ship glides across the ice.
annotation.walkthrough: The shrew is Katherina (Kate) from The Taming of the Shrew, set in Padua.
annotation.definitionFit: To skate is to glide across ice on blades.

entries.clue: Land in one piece meeting Benedictine? (6,7)

blocks.note: the king is a chess piece
Dom is the title of a Benedictine monk

annotation.surface: A monk arrives in the country safe and sound.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In one piece' looks like one phrase meaning intact; it splits into 'in one' and 'piece', a chessman. Dom is the title given to Benedictine monks.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the whole country of Britain and Northern Ireland is the land meant.

entries.clue: Unusual wheels beneath extremely durable object (5)

indicatorNotes.beneath: in a down clue, MUR sits below DE

blocks.note: the first and last letters of DURABLE

annotation.surface: A strange set of wheels under a very tough item.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Object' looks like a noun, a thing, but is the verb: to object is to demur. Rum is British for odd.
annotation.definitionFit: Here 'object' is the verb, to protest; demurring is voicing a mild objection.

entries.clue: Italian agreement reversed by the French — in Ireland? (4)

indicatorNotes.reversed: Reversed means turned the other way, so the Italian yes is written backwards.

annotation.surface: A European treaty between Italy and France, somehow concerning Ireland.
annotation.walkthrough: Ireland is an island, so an isle is what Ireland is 'in' — the question mark marks the definition by example.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example, flagged by the question mark: Ireland is an island, so the whole place is 'in' an isle.
annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a cryptic pointer: Ireland is an example of an ISLE.

entries.clue: William and Harry say they’re up for a fight? (5)

blocks.note: William and Harry are royal princes, each given a ducal title on marrying
slang for fists, which go up before a fight

annotation.surface: The two princes are spoiling for a scrap.
annotation.walkthrough: Dukes is slang for fists, perhaps from rhyming slang Duke of Yorks = forks = hands; William and Harry are the Dukes of Cambridge and of Sussex.
annotation.definitionFit: William and Harry are royal dukes; dukes are also fists.

entries.clue: Accompaniments for dish: order smells terrible! (9)

blocks.note: trim = order, as in 'in good trim'
to ming is British slang for to stink

annotation.surface: A diner complains that the side dishes served with the meal stink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ming' is British slang for a bad smell. The trimmings are the traditional extras with a roast, such as stuffing and gravy.
annotation.definitionFit: Trimmings are the side dishes that accompany a main dish.

entries.clue: Runs in Paris and is second — tries again? (7)

annotation.surface: A runner in Paris comes second and wonders about another go.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' applies to both 'and' and 'is'. The question mark admits that retesting is only loosely trying again.
annotation.definitionFit: To retest is to test again, and to try can mean to test.

entries.clue: Each woman endlessly causes pain (7)

blocks.note: any woman's name will do; minus L gives RACHE

annotation.surface: Every woman who goes on and on is a pain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' looks like it modifies 'causes'; it trims the woman's name. An earache is also British slang for being nagged.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym narrowed: an ache in the ear is one kind of pain, and the surface's nagging woman adds the slang sense.
